Series::sign¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series::sign() const -> Series
Series& Series::sign_() const

What It Does¶

Returns the elementwise sign summary.

For each element, sign() keeps only directional information:

  • negative values become -1

  • zero becomes 0

  • positive values become 1

This is the complement of Series::abs. abs() keeps magnitude and throws direction away; sign() keeps direction and throws magnitude away.

Parameters¶

None.

Returns¶

Series A new Series with the same shape as self, containing only sign-coded values.

Gradient¶

sign() is best taught as a discrete directional summary rather than a smooth differentiable transform. Its main use is value inspection, rule building, and piecewise control logic.

In-Place Form¶

sign_() is the in-place sibling of sign(): it computes the same result and writes it back into self directly — mutating it (and any other handle sharing the same storage) instead of allocating a new Series — then returns a reference to self.

Despite being declared const at the call site — a quirk of how this method’s wrapper is generated, not a promise that self is left unchanged — sign_() genuinely mutates the series it’s called on.

auto x = pluss::make_series({-3.0, 0.0, 4.0});

auto& ref = x.sign_();
std::cout << "x=" << x << "\n";
std::cout << std::boolalpha << "same object: " << (&ref == &x);

Output¶

x=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[-1, 0, 1]
same object: true

Examples¶

Example 1. Negative, zero, and positive values collapse to -1, 0, and 1.

auto base = pluss::make_series({
    {-3.0, -2.0, -1.0},
    {0.0, 1.0, 4.0},
});

pluss::series::print(std::cout, base.sign());

Output¶

Series(shape=[2,3], strides=[3,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=true)
data=
⎡ -1.0000 -1.0000 -1.0000 ⎤
⎣  0.0000  1.0000  1.0000 ⎦

Example 2. Integer inputs produce integer sign-coded outputs.

std::cout << pluss::make_series({-9, 0, 11}, pluss::ScalarType::Int64).sign();

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=int64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[-1, 0, 1]

Example 3. sign() can be a compact way to surface edge behavior, including special values.

std::cout << pluss::make_series({
    -1.0,
    0.0,
    1.0,
    std::numeric_limits<double>::quiet_NaN(),
}).sign();

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[-1, 0, 1, 0]

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • sign() intentionally discards magnitude. After this transform, 1000 and 1 are indistinguishable if they had the same sign.

  • On the verified NaN example above, the output slot is 0. That is worth calling out because users often expect either nan propagation or an error.

Summary¶

Use sign() when you need directional classification, not measurement. It is especially useful before branching into piecewise logic or when you want to summarize polarity without preserving scale.

See Also¶

  • Series::abs: magnitude without direction.

  • Series::neg: sign flip without losing magnitude.

  • Series::log: a domain-sensitive transform where sign often determines whether the call is meaningful.
